De-identify linked datasets with a profile

Source: R/anon_deidentify.R
anon_deidentify.Rd

Turns a list of SDTM and/or ADaM datasets (or other data described by a profile) into a copy whose measured re-identification risk meets a target, with as little damage as possible: it removes direct identifiers, pseudonymizes subjects, offsets their dates, generalizes quasi-identifiers up their ladders, and suppresses what remains.

Usage

anon_deidentify(
  data,
  profile = anon_profile_sdtm(),
  key = "USUBJID",
  max_risk = 0.09,
  max_suppressed = 0.05,
  unresolved = c("drop", "keep"),
  keep_secrets = FALSE,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, a named list of data frames linked by key, or the result of an earlier step.

profile

An anon_profile(), such as anon_profile_sdtm(), anon_profile_adam(), or both combined with c() for a list holding SDTM and ADaM datasets.

key

Name of the subject identifier column. It must be the profile's "key" rule, if it has one.

max_risk

Highest acceptable re-identification risk for any subject (the maximum risk, 1 / k for the smallest group). The target group size is the smallest k with 1 / k <= max_risk, allowing for floating-point error so that 0.1 and 1/3 give 10 and 3. The default, 0.09, is the threshold Health Canada and EMA encourage for public release of clinical information, and requires groups of at least 12. Health Canada equates 0.09 with a cell size of 11, but 1 / 11 is about 0.0909; to use groups of 11, pass max_risk = 1/11. See Details.

max_suppressed

Largest share of quasi-identifier cells (subjects times the measures of the quasi-identifiers that vary) that suppression may blank before the search stops generalizing; above it, the search climbs the ladders even when a step saves no cells. Default 0.05.

unresolved

What to do with subjects still in groups smaller than the target when nothing is left to blank: "drop" (default) removes them from every dataset, "keep" keeps them (see anon_suppress()).

keep_secrets

Logical. If TRUE, keep the pseudonym mapping, the date offsets and the folded categories; read them with anon_secrets(). Default FALSE: they are kept nowhere.

seed

Optional seed, for reproducible tests: the pseudonyms are drawn with seed and the date offsets with seed + 1. Anyone with the seed and the original data can rebuild the mapping and the offsets, so don't set it for data you share.

Value

An object of class "anon_deid_step" (see anon_subject_ids()), chainable with the other steps, with the steps' logs and settings (settings$deidentify for this function; deidentify_1 and so on when it runs again on its own result), the record of suppressed cells, and also risk_before and risk_after (from anon_risk()) and signals (a tibble with signal, dataset, n_subjects, n_unique, n_below_k and n_below_k_with_quasi). Secrets only with keep_secrets = TRUE.

Details

Steps.

  1. Direct identifiers ("remove" rules) are blanked in every row of the datasets and of the data frames nested in them (packed and list columns, at any depth); the columns are kept, with their type and attributes, so code that uses them still runs, but without value labels or missing-value codes, which can hold the identifier. An exact "remove" name found nowhere is noted in the log.

  2. anon_subject_ids() replaces the key, "also" and "key_cols" columns. A dataset without the key whose rows an "also" column ties to subjects (see anon_profile()) takes the key for these steps, and is released without it.

  3. anon_subject_dates() offsets every date of each subject by one random offset (its own detection: Date and date-time columns, and text columns named *DTC, at any depth); text columns matched by the profile's "date" rules (such as VISIT_DATE, in the datasets with the key) are offset by the same offsets, as *DTC columns are: values that aren't ISO 8601 dates (10MAR2021, 03/10/2021, --03-10) are removed, with a warning, and bare years move by whole years. So are those of the data frames nested in them, each row with the offset of the subject that owns it (rows no subject owns are blanked).

  4. The quasi-identifiers the profile finds are measured (anon_risk()). Each is measured from its source: the copy with one value per subject that holds a value for the most subjects. Every other copy that shows some subject another value than the source (such as WEIGHTBL from another visit than the vs baseline, or a copy holding subjects the source doesn't) is measured too, as a measure of its own: it is generalized at the quasi-identifier's level and suppressed like the others, so the released combination is what is measured. Copies are never overwritten with the source's values. A column copy with more than one value for a subject (such as AAGE across events) can't be measured: a warning names it, and the target is not met. A quasi-identifier with no copy that holds one value per subject can't be measured at all: a warning names it, it is released as it is, the variables derived from it are blanked, and the target is not met.

  5. Ladder search (greedy, as Datafly), on the measured values (one per subject and measure). The cost of a state is the cells suppression would blank, estimated with anon_suppress()'s algorithm (a subject it can't resolve counts as all its cells), plus every cell of a removed quasi-identifier. While above max_suppressed of the cells, or while a step lowers the cost, it takes one step up the ladder of the quasi-identifier whose next step costs least (ties: the step that loses the fewest distinct values, then profile order). When every ladder is exhausted above the budget, it keeps the state that cost least (the earliest on ties). Last, it steps back down wherever that doesn't raise the cost (most useful quasi-identifiers first), so steps taken on a plateau are undone. Each ladder step applies to the original values. A quasi-identifier with one value for every subject in every measure can't split a group: it is measured, but neither generalized nor suppressed.

  6. The chosen steps are applied to every copy of each quasi-identifier (anon_generalize(), in every dataset with the key that the rule covers; "remove" blanks every copy in every row), then anon_suppress() blanks what remains in every measure, with everywhere = TRUE and the profile's priorities as order (they break ties). Cells blanked in a source are blanked for the same subjects in its copies that aren't measured on their own (copies under another name, and test copies such as the WEIGHT rows of advs).

  7. Derived variables are kept where they still follow from the released values of their quasi-identifiers, and blanked elsewhere (below). Value labels of generalized or suppressed columns keep only the values still released. The risk is measured again.

Nested data. Columns of the data frames nested in a dataset with the key (packed columns and the data frames in list columns, at any depth) take the dataset's rules. Those of quasi-identifiers and derived variables are measured and changed like datasets of their own, each row with the subject that owns it (see anon_subject_ids()): a nested copy of AGE is generalized and suppressed with it, and measured on its own where it shows some subject another value. They are named after where they are, such as dm.extra for packed column extra of dm and dm.visits[[]] for the data frames in list column visits. Rows that no subject owns are blanked in those columns, and logged.

Derived variables. A derived variable is left as it is where no ladder step applies to its quasi-identifiers and the subject's cells of them weren't blanked. Otherwise (in every row, when a ladder step applies; whether a value happened to stay the same, as an age on a band's lower bound, doesn't matter), with one quasi-identifier in the same row (such as AGEGR1 with AGE in adsl):

  • from a text quasi-identifier (RACEN from RACE), it takes the value that the released value had in the original data (the code of "OTHER", say) when the original data maps each value to one derived value, and is blanked otherwise or where there is none;

  • from a numeric one (AGEGR1 from AGE), it takes a category only when the derived values are intervals of the quasi-identifier in the original data and every value the released one can stand for (all ages of a band, whole numbers when the original values are) lies within one category: between its lowest and highest observed values, the lowest category being open below and the highest above (between two categories, where the cut lies isn't known); otherwise it is blanked.

A derived variable with several quasi-identifiers (BMIBL), or whose quasi-identifiers aren't in the same row (the BMI parameter), is blanked in every row when a ladder step applies to one of them, and otherwise for the subjects whose cells of one of them were blanked; for a result column (AVAL, --STRESN), with the other results of the row. Blanking keeps values truthful: a derived value recomputed from a representative (such as a BMI from a rounded weight) would not be any subject's. from can name the column of a copy (AAGEGR1 from AAGE); a column copy named as the quasi-identifier (AGE rather than AAGE) is preferred. A derived value missing in the data stays missing. A derived variable whose from names a quasi-identifier that isn't measured (not in the data, or with no copy that can be measured, such as BMIBL without height and weight) is blanked in every row, with a warning.

When the target is met. settings$deidentify$meets_target is TRUE only when the risk measured on the released data meets the target and anon_suppress() found no other reason not to (copies of a quasi-identifier that differ, birth dates next to AGE, values of removed subjects left); reasons are in settings$deidentify$not_met. No quasi-identifier found in the data is a reason too. So is each kind of identifier or date that anon_subject_ids() and anon_subject_dates() name in their warnings as left in the data (their settings' findings): original keys or related IDs in other columns or inside text, columns named like an identifier in another case, datasets without the key holding identifiers or dates, dates that weren't shifted (dates inside free text, text dates outside *DTC and the profile's "date" rules, numbers with a SAS date format, bare years kept), objects that can't be de-identified, value labels holding keys or dates, and text that can't be searched. A date column that holds one value in every row (such as a dictionary version, "2019-09", in a dataset without the key) can't tell subjects apart and isn't a reason; identifiers always are. No date parser is guessed: SAS datetimes held as text in a result column (such as AVALC of the FPPDTM1 parameter of ADaM's ADAB) aren't shifted, are named in a warning, and the target is not met; remove them or convert them first. Last, an audit walks every dataset at every depth for what the steps left as it was, each kind named in a warning and a reason: columns, supplemental qualifiers and elements of list columns that look like quasi-identifiers without a rule (see anon_profile()); datasets without the key (and no "also" columns that tie their rows to subjects) holding columns the profile names or that look like quasi-identifiers; profile date columns that weren't offset (such as a number of days); quasi-identifier or derived columns holding lists, and elements of list columns that a rule matches; attributes of quasi-identifier, derived and test result columns other than those that describe them (label, formats, value labels and missing-value codes, class, levels, names, time zone and the type's structural attributes), which can hold their original values and are left as they are; and data frames held in attributes whose columns the profile names or that look like quasi-identifiers.

Residual signals. Meeting the target covers the quasi-identifiers (measured), and the identifiers and dates the steps find (above). Other things a person might know single subjects out too: treatment duration (the profile's "duration" rules, which offsetting doesn't change; in days and in the rule's bands), the number of rows a subject has in each dataset, the visits (VISITNUM, AVISITN) and study days (--DY, ADY) it has, the set of tests (--TESTCD, PARAMCD) it has, and, for each generalized test, the set of its released values across all rows (such as weights at every visit, not only the measured baseline). Columns that hold a duration exactly (TRTDURD, ADURN, --DUR) are kept and not measured. signals counts, for each, the subjects unique on it alone and in groups smaller than the target, alone and together with the released quasi-identifiers. They are measured, not changed (changing dates would break study days). When subjects are in small groups on them, the copy is not anonymous against someone who knows them: say so wherever it is shared.

The log has rows for every step and every ladder move, with counts and no values; the settings hold the profile (as text), the levels chosen, the risk before and after and the residual signals.

Meeting the target is evidence about re-identification risk from the profile's quasi-identifiers, not proof that the data is anonymous under any regime (see anon_risk()). Shifted dates do not meet HIPAA Safe Harbor.

See also

anon_profile(), anon_risk(), anon_generalize(), anon_suppress()

Examples

dm <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = sprintf("S%02d", 1:12),
  AGE = c(31, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 52, 55, 58, 61, 66, 69),
  SEX = rep(c("F", "M"), 6),
  RFSTDTC = format(as.Date("2020-01-01") + 0:11)
)
result <- anon_deidentify(list(dm = dm), max_risk = 1/3, seed = 1)
result$data$dm
#>    USUBJID AGE SEX    RFSTDTC
#> 1  SUBJ-01  40   M 2019-09-17
#> 2  SUBJ-02  40   F 2019-10-12
#> 3  SUBJ-03  40   F 2020-11-04
#> 4  SUBJ-04  NA   M 2019-11-21
#> 5  SUBJ-05  40   M 2020-08-26
#> 6  SUBJ-06  40   F 2019-10-27
#> 7  SUBJ-07  NA   F 2020-11-24
#> 8  SUBJ-08  40   M 2019-04-03
#> 9  SUBJ-09  NA   F 2019-01-30
#> 10 SUBJ-10  NA   M 2019-07-01
#> 11 SUBJ-11  NA   M 2019-08-06
#> 12 SUBJ-12  NA   F 2019-07-22
result$settings$deidentify$meets_target
#> [1] TRUE
